title: Mobile App Lifecycle & Process Model
summary: Every mobile OS models your app as active, background, suspended, or killed — and can end the killed state without asking. Learn the shared mental model before the Android/iOS specifics.

slides.markdown:
A desktop app that isn't focused just sits idle in RAM, waiting. A mobile app doesn't get that courtesy: the OS treats it as a resource to reclaim the instant something more important needs memory.

Every mobile platform models your app through the same four states — **active, background, suspended, killed** — and the same brutal rule: the OS can move you toward "killed" without a warning, a callback, or your consent. Cold start, warm start, state restoration, and "what survives a kill" all follow from that one fact.

This topic is the cross-platform mental model. The exact callback names (`onPause`, `applicationDidEnterBackground`) belong to the Android and iOS groups.

slides.sectionTitle: The four states every mobile OS models
slides.markdown:
Strip away platform-specific names and every mobile OS is really asking one question about your process: **how visible and how trustworthy is it right now?**

- **Active (foreground)** — on screen, receiving input, running at full priority.
- **Background (running)** — not visible, but still an active process with a limited execution budget (a timer, a short task, a few seconds of audio playback).
- **Suspended (frozen)** — still resident in memory, but the OS has frozen its execution entirely. No code runs. It's a memory snapshot, not a live process.
- **Killed (terminated)** — the process is gone. Memory is reclaimed. Restarting means a fresh process from scratch.

The OS moves you down this ladder as memory pressure rises, and it moves fastest for apps it judges least important — the one you haven't touched in three days loses first.

slides.sectionTitle: Why phones kill processes without asking
slides.markdown:
A phone has no swap file worth relying on and a battery it must protect, so both memory and CPU are scarce in a way a server never experiences. The OS's job is to keep the **foreground app buttery smooth**, and it will sacrifice anything else to do that.

When free memory drops below a threshold, a low-memory killer walks the list of background and suspended processes, ranked by recency and importance, and terminates the least valuable ones — no `SIGTERM` grace period you can rely on, no notification to your app.

This isn't a bug to work around. It's the load-bearing assumption of mobile development: **your process can disappear at any moment it isn't on screen**, and your app has to behave as if that's normal, because it is.

slides.subTitle: What actually moves you between states
slides.markdown:
Each transition has a concrete trigger, not a vague "sometimes":

- **Active → Background**: the user presses home, switches apps, or a system dialog (incoming call) takes focus.
- **Background → Suspended**: your background execution budget runs out, or the OS decides to freeze you proactively to save power.
- **Suspended → Killed**: memory pressure crosses a threshold and the low-memory killer reclaims your process.
- **Killed/Suspended → Active**: the user taps your icon or a notification. If killed, this is a **cold start**; if suspended, the OS just unfreezes and resumes — no relaunch needed.

The important asymmetry: going down this ladder can skip steps (a phone call can suspend you directly), but coming back up from "killed" always means rebuilding from nothing.

![Four-state app process ladder from Active down to Killed with a cold-start arrow back](assets/app-process-state-ladder.svg)

assets.alt: Four-state app process ladder from Active down to Killed with a cold-start arrow back

slides.markdown:
In the foreground you get effectively unlimited CPU, as much network as you want, and no time limit — you're the thing the user is looking at, so the OS spends resources freely on you.

The moment you background, that budget shrinks hard. Both Android and iOS give you a short window — historically on the order of **seconds to low tens of seconds** — to finish critical work (flush a write, cancel a request, save state) before you're either suspended or throttled to near-zero CPU.

Anything that needs to keep running longer than that window has to explicitly ask the OS for permission through a background-task API, and even then the OS can revoke it under memory or battery pressure. There's no way to just "keep working quietly" — the budget is enforced, not a suggestion.

slides.sectionTitle: Rebuilding UI after a process death
slides.subTitle: State restoration
slides.markdown:
When the user taps back into a killed app, the OS can often make it *look* like nothing happened — same screen, same scroll position — even though the process is brand new. That illusion is called **state restoration**, and it's on you to build it.

The pattern is the same everywhere: before you're suspended, serialize the minimum needed to reconstruct the screen (a navigation stack, a scroll offset, a form draft, an item ID — never the full object graph) to durable storage. On relaunch, check for that saved state before doing anything else and rebuild the UI from it instead of showing the default launch screen.

Users read a broken restoration as **data loss**, even when nothing was technically lost — the form they were filling in just vanished. Treat restoration as a core feature, not an edge case.

slides.sectionTitle: Cold start vs warm start vs hot start
slides.markdown:
"Launching the app" means three very different things depending on what state the OS found it in:

| Start type | Process | Work required | Typical feel |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cold** | Killed, must be spawned | Load process, run init code, restore state, first render | Slowest — hundreds of ms to seconds |
| **Warm** | Process alive, activity/view destroyed | Recreate the UI from existing process + saved state | Faster — skips process + full init |
| **Hot** | Process and UI both alive, just suspended | Resume from memory, no rebuild | Near-instant |

Performance work targets these differently: cold start is an app-init problem (defer work off the critical path), warm start is a UI-recreation problem (cheap view construction), and hot start usually needs no work at all. Profiling tools report these as separate metrics precisely because the fixes don't transfer between them.

slides.sectionTitle: What actually persists across a kill
slides.markdown:
A process kill wipes everything that lived in that process's memory. That's a shorter list than most people assume:

- **Gone**: in-memory variables, singletons, static caches, open network connections and sockets, unsaved in-flight state, anything held only in a ViewModel or its equivalent.
- **Survives**: anything you explicitly wrote to disk — a database row, a file, a key-value store entry, an OS-provided "saved state" bundle you populated yourself, and scheduled background jobs registered with the OS (they wake a fresh process to run).

The rule of thumb: **the OS remembers that you asked it to do something later; it does not remember what you were thinking**. If a value needs to exist after a possible kill, you must have written it somewhere durable before the kill happened — there's no way to recover it after the fact.

The most common lifecycle bug: code that assumes going to background just pauses execution in place, like minimizing a desktop window, and picks up exactly where it left off.

In reality, backgrounding starts a countdown. A network callback that fires after you've backgrounded may run with a UI that no longer exists to update, or may never run at all if you're suspended mid-request. A timer or animation that assumes it keeps ticking will instead find itself frozen for an arbitrary length of time and then resumed with a huge, nonsensical elapsed-time value.

The defensive pattern is always the same: on the way to background, cancel or checkpoint anything in flight; on the way back to foreground, re-validate state rather than assuming it's still fresh (a cached price, an auth token, a location fix) instead of blindly resuming.

slides.sectionTitle: Never testing restoration because it rarely happens on a dev device
slides.markdown:
Your development phone has 12GB of RAM and one app open. Real users have forty apps, three years of accumulated storage pressure, and an entry-level device with a quarter of your RAM — their instance of your app gets killed constantly, often within seconds of backgrounding.

Because a dev device almost never reaches that memory pressure, process death and restoration go untested for entire release cycles, and the bug only surfaces in a support ticket: "the app forgot what I was doing."

Both Android and iOS ship a developer option to force-kill a backgrounded process on demand specifically because of this gap. Make it part of your manual test pass for any screen that holds meaningful in-progress state — a multi-step form, a checkout flow, a draft — not just an occasional spot check.
